title: Nakshatra and Pada
subtitle: Understanding the twenty-seven lunar mansions and their four quarters
summary: This session introduces Nakshatra as the Moon's position within twenty-seven equal divisions of the zodiac. Students learn that each Nakshatra spans 13°20′, each Pada spans 3°20′, how to calculate the running Nakshatra and Pada from sidereal longitude, the sequence of the twenty-seven Nakshatras, and why Nakshatra is important in Panchang and birth-chart interpretation.
learningObjectives: Define Nakshatra as one of twenty-seven equal divisions of the zodiac.
Explain why each Nakshatra contains four Padas of 3°20′ each.
Name the twenty-seven Nakshatras in sequence.
Calculate the running Nakshatra from sidereal longitude.
Calculate the Pada within a Nakshatra.
Understand the foundation-level role of Janma Nakshatra.
prerequisites: Completion of Session 5: Vara and Weekday Lords.
Basic understanding of the 360° zodiac and sidereal longitude.

blocks.text: Nakshatra is the twenty-seven-part division of the zodiac used to track the Moon's position against the sidereal sky. Because the Moon moves relatively quickly, its Nakshatra usually changes approximately once per day, though the exact duration varies.

blocks.explanation: The full zodiac is divided into twenty-seven equal lunar mansions.
blocks.workedExample: Ashwini spans 0°00′ to 13°20′ of the chosen sidereal zodiac.

blocks.altText: A simple monochrome zodiac wheel divided into twenty-seven equal Nakshatra sectors.
blocks.caption: The 360° zodiac is divided into twenty-seven equal Nakshatras.
blocks.purpose: Show the complete Nakshatra grid as a uniform division of the zodiac.

blocks.title: Nakshatra is based on longitude
blocks.text: For Panchang calculation, the running Nakshatra is identified from the Moon's sidereal longitude.

blocks.caption: The twenty-seven Nakshatras in order
blocks.note: The nine planetary lords repeat three times through the twenty-seven Nakshatras.

blocks.title: Sequence matters
blocks.text: The Nakshatra order is fixed and is used directly in Dasha calculation and several later rules.

blocks.explanation: Each Nakshatra is divided into four equal quarters.
blocks.workedExample: The first Pada of Ashwini spans 0°00′ to 3°20′.

blocks.altText: A single Nakshatra arc divided into four equal Padas of 3°20′ each.
blocks.caption: Every Nakshatra contains four equal Padas.
blocks.purpose: Connect Nakshatra span to Pada calculation.

blocks.title: Four Padas per Nakshatra
blocks.text: Twenty-seven Nakshatras multiplied by four Padas gives 108 Padas across the zodiac.

sections.title: How to Calculate the Running Nakshatra

blocks.workedExample: A Moon longitude of 45° lies in the fourth Nakshatra, Rohini.

blocks.title: Find the running Nakshatra
steps: Convert one Nakshatra to decimal degrees: 13°20′ = 13.333...°.

blocks.title: Use the correct zodiac framework
blocks.text: Do not mix tropical longitude with a sidereal Nakshatra table. Use the selected Ayanamsha consistently.

blocks.expression: Position within Nakshatra = Moon longitude mod 13°20′
blocks.explanation: This gives the Moon's distance from the beginning of the current Nakshatra.
blocks.workedExample: If the remainder is 7°10′, the Moon lies in the third Pada.
7°10′ ÷ 3°20′ gives two complete Pada intervals, so the Pada index is 3.

blocks.title: Nakshatra and Pada together
blocks.scenario: The Moon is at 18°10′ of the sidereal zodiac.
steps: Ashwini ends at 13°20′, so the Moon is in Bharani.
blocks.conclusion: The Moon is in Bharani, Pada 2.

sections.title: Nakshatra and Rashi Are Different Grids

blocks.title: Two divisions of the same zodiac

left.label: Rashi grid
points: Used for sign placement and house-based interpretation.

right.label: Nakshatra grid
points: Used in Panchang, Dasha and lunar-based interpretation.

blocks.altText: Two aligned horizontal scales showing twelve Rashis and twenty-seven Nakshatras across the same 360° zodiac.
blocks.caption: Rashi and Nakshatra are different grids placed over the same zodiac.
blocks.purpose: Prevent the common mistake of treating one Nakshatra as equal to one Rashi.

blocks.title: Their boundaries do not always match
blocks.text: Some Nakshatras lie entirely within one Rashi, while others cross a Rashi boundary.

Janma Nakshatra is the Nakshatra occupied by the Moon at birth. It is widely used in naming traditions, Vimshottari Dasha starting calculations, compatibility systems and several interpretive frameworks.

items: Use the remaining arc within the Nakshatra for later Dasha-balance calculation.

blocks.title: Do not reduce a person to one Nakshatra
blocks.text: Janma Nakshatra is important, but complete interpretation requires the full chart, planetary strength, houses, aspects and Dasha context.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming one Nakshatra equals one Rashi.
commonMistakes.whyItIsWrong: A Rashi spans 30°, while a Nakshatra spans 13°20′.
commonMistakes.correctUnderstanding: Treat them as two different divisions of the same zodiac.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using tropical longitude directly for a sidereal Nakshatra table.
commonMistakes.whyItIsWrong: Nakshatra calculation depends on the selected sidereal framework.

commonMistakes.mistake: Forgetting to add 1 after taking the floor value.
commonMistakes.whyItIsWrong: The mathematical quotient starts from zero, while Nakshatra numbering starts from one.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating Pada as a separate Nakshatra.
commonMistakes.whyItIsWrong: A Pada is one quarter of the current Nakshatra.

commonMistakes.mistake: Making a full personality judgement from Janma Nakshatra alone.
commonMistakes.whyItIsWrong: Nakshatra is one part of a complete chart.
commonMistakes.correctUnderstanding: Use it together with the full Kundali and timing context.

sessionSummary: The zodiac is divided into twenty-seven Nakshatras.
Each Nakshatra contains four Padas of 3°20′ each.
There are 108 Padas across the zodiac.
The running Nakshatra is calculated from the Moon's sidereal longitude.
The Pada is calculated from the Moon's position within the current Nakshatra.
Rashi and Nakshatra are different grids over the same 360° zodiac.
The twenty-seven Nakshatras follow a fixed sequence.
Janma Nakshatra is the Moon's Nakshatra at birth.
Complete interpretation should not rely on Nakshatra alone.

questions.question: How many Nakshatras divide the zodiac?
questions.explanation: The traditional Nakshatra grid divides 360° into twenty-seven equal parts.

questions.question: What is the span of one Nakshatra?
What is the span of one Pada?
questions.explanation: Each Nakshatra is divided into four equal Padas.

questions.question: One Nakshatra is equal to one Rashi.
questions.explanation: A Nakshatra spans 13°20′ and a Rashi spans 30°.

questions.question: What is Janma Nakshatra?
questions.answer: The Nakshatra occupied by the Moon at birth.
questions.explanation: It is calculated from the Moon's sidereal longitude at birth.

questions.question: Which Nakshatra follows Rohini?
questions.explanation: The sequence is Krittika, Rohini, Mrigashira and Ardra.

questions.question: There are 108 Padas across the twenty-seven Nakshatras.
Why must the selected Ayanamsha be used consistently?
questions.answer: Because changing the sidereal reference can change the calculated Nakshatra near a boundary.
